verses.translation_literal: And God remembered [obj] Noah and [obj] every living creature and [obj] all the livestock which [were] with him in the ark; and God made a wind pass over the earth, and the waters subsided.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then God remembered Noah. Through all the long dark, with the rain-drummed hull creaking and the animals shifting in their stalls, he had not been forgotten, and now the remembering moved. God turned toward Noah, toward every living creature, toward every beast of the herd that shared the ark with him. And God sent a wind sweeping across the face of the earth. The great waters, so long heaving and unbroken, began to settle and sink.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Remembered' is not a recovered memory. In the Hebrew world, to remember (zakhar) is to act on a bond: God turns toward Noah and does something about him. Radak says as much: there is no forgetting before God, and the Torah speaks in human language so that its hearers can understand, as in 'I will remember my covenant' (Lev 26). Play it as a turn, not a thought.

The list matters: Noah first, then 'every living creature' and 'all the livestock'. The animals are inside the remembering. Ramban says they are not remembered for merit, since only humans have merit or guilt, but because God keeps His word about the world's continuity.

The KJV 'asswaged' is archaic English for 'calmed, lessened'; the Hebrew shakhakh is the word used of the king's anger cooling in Esther 7:10, as Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all note. The waters are not drained but quieted, like a rage. The KJV also says 'every living thing', flattening chayyah, 'living creature' or 'wild animal', and 'God made a wind to pass', which keeps the causative well. The word ruach also means 'spirit'; the echo of Gen 1:2 is tempting but the text does not say it.

philological_notes.note: 'Remember' in the Bible means to turn toward and act, not merely to recall. Radak stresses that God has no forgetting and that the language is human.
To subside, to grow calm; used of the king's wrath cooling in Esther 7:10. The image is of anger quieting.

verses.translation_literal: And the springs of the deep were shut up, and the floodgates of the heavens, and the rain was restrained from the heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: The springs of the deep were sealed. The floodgates of the sky were shut. And the rain, which had fallen without mercy, was held back from the heavens.
verses.directors_commentary:
This undoes 7:11 step by step: there the springs of the great deep burst open and the 'floodgates of the heavens' opened; here both close, and the rain is held back. The flood was cosmic plumbing, water from below and water from above, and the actors should feel a valve turning.

The KJV 'windows of heaven' is not wrong but misleading; arubbah means a lattice or sluice, an opening in a ceiling (the same word is used of a chimney-hole or a dove-cote). Rashi notes that in 7:11 it says 'all the springs' and here it does not say 'all', because the useful springs, such as hot springs, remained. 'Stopped' (sakar) is simply 'shut'; Ibn Ezra takes it as the same as sagar. The passive 'was restrained' (kala) means held back, as in 'do not hold back your mercies' (Ps 40:12), Rashi says.

philological_notes.note: Lattice, sluice-opening; KJV 'windows' is a loose rendering of an architectural term for an opening that lets something through.
Niphal: was held back, shut in. Rashi compares 'do not withhold your mercies' (Ps 40:12).

verses.translation_literal: And the waters turned back from upon the earth, going and turning back; and the waters decreased from the end of a hundred and fifty days.
verses.translation_dramatic: Slowly, slowly the waters drew back from the earth, going and returning, going and returning, like a tide that cannot make up its mind. And when a hundred and fifty days had run their course, the waters were less.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew uses the same root twice: the waters 'turned back' (vayashuvu) 'going and turning back' (halokh vashov). It is an ebb that does not run in a straight line, the pulse of a receding sea. The KJV 'continually' loses the double motion, and 'after the end of the hundred and fifty days' adds a definite article and an 'after'; the Hebrew says 'from the end of' (miqtseh), the point at which the decrease is counted.

The dating is a famous puzzle. Rashi counts from the end of the rain, Radak and Ramban argue about when the 150 days begin and which months are meant; Ibn Ezra rejects some of the attempts. Do not stage a calendar: the count of 150 days is the steady measure of how long the high water held and then began to ebb.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolutes, 'going and returning': a repeated, gradual motion rather than a single draining. Radak: little by little.
To lack, to decrease; the opposite of the water 'prevailing' earlier. KJV 'abated' is acceptable.

verses.translation_literal: And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat.
verses.translation_dramatic: And in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day, the ark came to rest, a long groan of timber and then stillness, upon the mountains of Ararat.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Rested' is vattanach, from the root nuach, the same root as the name Noah (Noach). The man who was named for rest (5:29) sees his vessel come to rest. The KJV preserves 'rested' but, like all English, cannot make the sound play visible.

The Hebrew says 'mountains' in the plural: harei Ararat, a range, not a single peak. Ararat is the land of Urartu, in the highlands north of Mesopotamia; the text does not name one summit. Radak even doubts that these were the highest mountains, and Ramban worries about how the arithmetic of depth and date can work. The seventh month and the seventeenth day are given plainly; treat them as the arrival of a long-awaited, tiny fact.

philological_notes.note: To settle, to come to rest. It shares its root with the name Noah and with manoach in 8:9.
'Mountains of Ararat', plural: a range in the land of Urartu. The text names no single mountain.

verses.translation_literal: And the waters were going and decreasing until the tenth month; in the tenth [month], on the first of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the waters kept going down, going down, until the tenth month. And on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains were seen, dark and dripping against the sky.
verses.directors_commentary:
Same pair of verbs as in 8:3, 'going and decreasing' (halokh vechasor): a slow, patient ebb. Then the first sight of land, on the first of the month, and it is only the 'heads' (rashei) of the mountains, a word that also means 'tops' but is literally 'heads', as if the earth were surfacing for breath.

The KJV 'decreased continually' flattens the repeated infinitives; 'were the tops of the mountains seen' keeps the Hebrew passive nir'u, 'they were seen', so that we do not learn who saw them. Ibn Ezra observes that Noah could not have seen the new moon, since the window was still closed: the first of the month is the text's count, not necessarily Noah's. The commentators dispute whether the tenth month counts from the rain or from the end of the rain (Rashi, Ramban, Radak).

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolutes: a continuing, gradual decrease. Radak compares 'the living creatures ran and returned' (Ezek 1:14).
'Heads' or 'tops'; the same word as 'head'. Radak: the highest places of the mountains.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, from the end of forty days, and Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made.
verses.translation_dramatic: Forty days passed. Then Noah opened the window of the ark, the one he himself had made.
verses.directors_commentary:
Noah acts at last. 'The ark which he had made' is a small, loaded phrase: his own craftsmanship, and now his own hand opening it. The KJV 'it came to pass' is the archaic rendering of the ordinary narrative marker vayehi.

The word here is challon, 'window', not the tsohar of 6:16; Rashi and Radak take the two as the same opening, Rashi distinguishing it from the door. The forty days are counted by Rashi from the sight of the mountains, by Radak from the ark coming to rest. Radak also explains his delay: Noah feared that the waves might rise in through the window.

philological_notes.note: 'Window', an opening. In 6:16 the ark's opening is called tsohar; Rashi and Radak identify it with this window.

verses.translation_literal: And he sent out the raven, and it went out, going out and returning, until the drying of the waters from upon the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: He sent out the raven. It went out, and went out, and came back, and went out again, a black speck against the pale sky, until the waters had dried from the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew says the raven 'went out, going out and returning' (yatso vashov) and stops. It does not say that the raven came back to the ark. That is why the commentators divide: Rashi says it circled the ark and would not go on Noah's errand, because it suspected him of wanting its mate; Radak says it went to and from its nest; Sforno says the air was still too much for it. The KJV 'to and fro' tilts toward the first view and the BBE 'this way and that' is also an interpretation.

After the flood, the 'drying' (yevoshet) of the waters is a final, distant point; the raven's flights are the audience's first clock for that slow drying. The raven eats carrion, as Radak says: Noah expected it to bring back something from the corpses. Ancient sailors in the Near East are known to have used birds as land-finders, though the text does not say so. Rashi also connects the raven to Elijah's ravens in 1 Kings 17, a thread that matters in this corpus.

philological_notes.note: 'Going out and returning'. The text does not say where the raven returned to; the commentators differ (circling the ark, to its nest, unable to bear the air).

'The raven', a scavenger. Radak's reasoning: it would find carrion if the earth were bare. The consonants of 'orev match those of 'erev 'evening' and 'arav 'to mix', which is my own observation, not a claim of the text.

verses.translation_literal: And he sent out the dove from with him, to see whether the waters had lightened from upon the face of the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then he sent out the dove, away from his own hand, to see whether the waters had grown light upon the face of the ground.
verses.directors_commentary:
'From with him' (me'ito) is tender and exact: the dove leaves his company. The key verb is qalu, 'were light': the waters have become light, not heavy, a word from the root qalal. The KJV 'abated' and the BBE 'gone' translate the result and lose the image of weight lifting; the Hebrew weighs.

The question is a real question: the interrogative ha- ('whether') opens it, and the dove is the instrument of an uncertain answer. Rashi hears in 'sent' the sense of letting her go her way: if she finds a resting place, she will not return. Sforno adds that she would nest in mountains and towers as is her custom. 'The ground' (adamah) is the soil, the same stuff from which the human was made, rather than the more general 'earth' (erets) of the previous verses.

philological_notes.note: 'Were they light?': the waters have grown light, with the same root as 'cursed' in other binyanim; here simply 'lightened, lessened'. Radak (8:11) says that what is less is called light, what is more is called heavy.
'The ground', arable soil, as distinct from erets 'earth'. My reading; the contrast is not made by the commentators in the packet.

verses.translation_literal: And the dove did not find a resting place for the sole of her foot, and she returned to him, to the ark, for water [was] upon the face of all the earth; and he sent out his hand and took her and brought her to him, to the ark.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the dove found nowhere to set down the sole of her foot. There was no resting place, only water, water to every edge of the world. So she came back to him, back to the ark. And Noah stretched out his hand, and took her, and drew her in to himself, into the ark.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Resting place' is manoach, from nuach, the root of 'Noah' and of 'the ark rested' in 8:4. Noah himself is the one place of rest that the dove can find. The image of 'the sole of her foot' is tender and concrete: a bird no bigger than a hand, her foot with nowhere to fall.

The KJV 'pulled her in' is more vigorous than the Hebrew: vayave otah, 'and he brought her'. The double 'to him, to the ark' (elav el hateivah) is a small stutter: Radak reads 'to him' as returning to the sender with nothing, and 'to the ark' as resting on the roof of the ark without entering. Ramban says doves do not rest on bare peaks, which is why she found no place even though the tops were visible. Noah reaches out and takes her: the whole story of the flood is in that hand.

philological_notes.note: A resting place. Same root as Noach (Noah) and vattanach (8:4).
'To him, to the ark.' Radak distinguishes returning to the sender from reaching the ark.

verses.translation_literal: And he waited again seven other days, and he added to send out the dove from the ark.
verses.translation_dramatic: He waited again, another seven days. Then once more he sent the dove out from the ark.
verses.directors_commentary:
A week of waiting. 'Other seven days' (shiv'at yamim acherim) implies that the first wait, before the dove's first flight in 8:8, was also seven days, as Rashi and Radak infer from the word 'other'. The text never says so directly.

The verb vayachel, 'he waited', is a rare form; Rashi takes it as 'he waited', Ibn Ezra finds it odd, and Radak derives it from chul and notes the same form in Judg 3:25 ('they waited until they were ashamed'). The KJV 'stayed' is serviceable. 'He added to send' (vayoseph shalach) is the biblical way of saying 'he did it again'; the KJV 'again he sent' keeps the sense but not the 'adding'. The seven-day rhythm gives the passage the beat of a patient ritual.

philological_notes.note: 'He waited'. Rashi: a word of waiting, as in Job 29:21. Ibn Ezra thinks the form is irregular. Radak: from chul, like Judg 3:25.
'He added to send': an idiom for repeating an action.

verses.translation_literal: And the dove came to him at evening time, and behold, a freshly plucked leaf of an olive [was] in her mouth; and Noah knew that the waters had lightened from upon the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the dove came back to him at evening, when the light was going. And there, in her mouth, was an olive leaf, freshly plucked. And Noah knew. The waters had grown light upon the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'behold' (vehineh) puts the audience into Noah's eyes: the leaf is a discovery, seen at the moment he sees it. The olive leaf, taraf, is 'freshly plucked': Radak says it shows that the dove tore it from a tree, not found it floating. An olive tree thus stood above the water, and in the Hebrew world the olive is a tree of peace and oil.

The KJV 'pluckt off' is acceptable, though the Hebrew is a single word whose form puzzles the commentators. Rashi reads 'torn off, snatched', and notes that taraf can also mean food, which leads to the midrash that the dove said 'let my food be bitter as an olive from God's hand rather than sweet as honey from the hand of flesh and blood.' Ramban pushes back: this is homily, not the plain sense. Rashi also guesses that the dove here is male, since the word is masculine in form, but Ramban rejects that.

Noah 'knew' (vayeda) because the waters were 'light' again (qalu), the very word of 8:8. The question asked there is now answered, in the same vocabulary.

philological_notes.note: 'Freshly plucked, torn off.' Radak takes it as a passive adjective like taruf, meaning that the dove tore it from the tree. Rashi gives 'snatched', with an aggadic reading of 'food'. Ramban rejects the aggadic reading as homily.
'They were light': the answer to the question of 8:8. Radak: what is lessened is called light.

verses.translation_literal: And he waited again seven other days, and he sent out the dove, and she did not add to return to him again.
verses.translation_dramatic: Again he waited seven days. Again he sent out the dove. And this time she did not come back to him. Not ever again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The silence is the answer. The dove 'did not add' (lo yasfah) to return: the same verb of adding that Noah used in 8:10. The KJV 'returned not again unto him any more' is clear, but the Hebrew has a double 'again' (yasfah, od) that makes the absence final. Radak says Noah understood from it that the ground was dry and the dove had found a resting place on the earth and its many trees.

The verb of waiting here, vayiyachel, is a different form from 8:10's vayachel: Rashi and Ibn Ezra treat it as a passive or reflexive form (he let himself wait), and the commentators dispute its binyan. For an actor it is enough that the waiting is now longer than any before, with no news at the end of it.

philological_notes.note: A variant form of 'he waited'. Rashi calls it a reflexive, 'he held himself back'; Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as a Niphal of the root y-ch-l.
'She did not add': the idiom for 'she did not do it again'. Echoes the 'he added' of 8:10.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, in the one and six-hundredth year, in the first [month], on the first of the month, the waters were dry from upon the earth; and Noah removed the covering of the ark and saw, and behold, the face of the ground was dry.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the six hundred and first year of Noah's life, on the first day of the first month, the waters had gone from the earth. Noah drew back the covering of the ark. He looked out. And there — the face of the ground, dry.
verses.directors_commentary:
Noah has waited. He is not told to open the roof; he does it himself, and the text lets us watch him do it: removed, saw, 'and behold' — the Hebrew hinneh puts us behind his eyes. Play it as a man who has been shut in for months with a family and a menagerie, and who for the first time sees something that is not water.

KJV is right to keep 'the covering', but it flattens a distinction the Hebrew draws. Verse 13 says the waters and the ground ḥārəbû, 'dried out', and verse 14, a month and more later, says the earth yābəšâ, 'was dry'. KJV uses 'dried' for both and the difference vanishes. Rashi reads ḥārēb as a crust forming over mud; Radak agrees that the surface was dry while underneath it was still mire, which is why Noah is not yet sent out. Ibn Ezra says the same: the foot could not tread on it. That is the logic of the next verse.

Timekeeping: this is an exact calendar date, 1st of the first month, 601st year, in the same precise style as the flood's start in 7:11. Whether the first month is autumn (Tishri, R. Eliezer, Radak) or spring (Nisan, R. Joshua) is argued in Rashi; the text itself does not say. 'Face of the ground' (pənê hāʾădāmâ) is the ordinary idiom, and ʾădāmâ is the soil, the farmland, the stuff Adam was named from.

philological_notes.note: 'Were dried out, drained'. The verb is used of the waters and of the ground's surface, and is distinct from yābēš 'be dry' in v14. Rashi reads it as the surface crusting over like clay; Radak says the ground remained mud beneath.
'Covering', the roof or hatch material of the ark. The same noun is used for the tabernacle's coverings. Noah removes it himself; no command is given.

verses.translation_literal: And in the second month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, the earth was dry.
verses.translation_dramatic: And in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day, the earth was dry. Not a crust over mud. Dry.
verses.directors_commentary:
A bare date and a bare verb; let the silence carry it. After the careful 'dried out' of verse 13 comes a stronger word, yābəšâ, 'was dry', the word used for the dry land in Genesis 1:9–10. KJV renders it 'was the earth dried', which reads like the same event as the verse before. Rashi spells out the difference: now the ground has become fully dry, 'as it should be'.

Count the days: the flood began on the 17th of the second month (7:11); this is the 27th of the second month a year later, a year and ten days. Rashi and Radak, following Genesis Rabbah, explain the extra days as the solar year's surplus over a lunar year, so that the judgment lasted a full solar year. That is a rabbinic harmonization, not something the Hebrew says. What the text does give is a precise inventory of time: the ark was shut for well over a year.

philological_notes.note: 'Was dry, was arid': the word of Genesis 1:9–10 (yabbāšâ, dry land). It marks the completion of what ḥārəbû in v13 only began.

verses.translation_literal: And God spoke to Noah, saying:
verses.translation_dramatic: And God spoke to Noah. He said:
verses.directors_commentary:
Noah has seen dry ground and does nothing. He opens a hatch, not a door; he does not leave. He waits for the word that shut him in to be the word that lets him out. Play the pause: God speaks only now, after the full year and the full drying.

Note the divine name. The flood story has used both Elohim and YHWH; here it is Elohim who commands, and only at the altar in verse 20 does YHWH appear. KJV prints 'God' here and 'LORD' there, which is faithful, but it does not tell the reader that this is a shift. The formula 'saying' (lēʾmōr) introduces what follows; Rashbam notes that it doubles the verb of speech, a formal marker, not a second act.

philological_notes.note: Lit. 'to say', the quotation formula. Rashbam says every 'saying' in the Torah doubles a verb of command, calling, speaking or saying.

verses.translation_literal: Go out from the ark, you and your wife and your sons and your sons' wives with you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Go out. Out of the ark — you, and your wife, and your sons, and your sons' wives with you.
verses.directors_commentary:
One word, ṣēʾ, 'go out', ends the longest confinement in the book. Say it plainly, as an order, not a flourish.

The list repeats the entry list of 6:18, but with one change that Rashi and Radak both catch. When they entered, the sexes were listed apart (the men, then the women); now the text pairs 'you and your wife', then 'your sons and your sons' wives'. Rashi and Radak say that cohabitation, forbidden in the ark, is permitted again. That is a rabbinic reading of the shift in order, not something the Hebrew states, but the shift is real and an actor can use it. KJV, copying the Hebrew order, has the pairing but nothing signals that it matters.

philological_notes.note: Husbands and wives named together after the men and women were listed separately on entering; read by Rashi and Radak as permission to resume marital life.

verses.translation_literal: Every living thing that [is] with you, of all flesh, among the birds and among the livestock and among every creeper that creeps on the earth, bring out with you; and let them swarm in the earth and be fruitful and multiply on the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every living creature that is with you, all that is flesh — the birds, the livestock, every creeping thing that crawls upon the earth — bring them out with you. Let them swarm across the land. Let them be fruitful. Let them multiply upon the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a command to repopulate, and its sound is the point: three verbs in a row, 'swarm', 'be fruitful', 'multiply', with the earth named twice. Read it as a blessing with the energy of a release.

The verb šāraṣ 'swarm' is the one Genesis 1:20 used of the waters teeming with fish; it is not the usual word for land animals. Radak notes that the land animals, few now, get the strongest language of increase: swarm, be fruitful and multiply. KJV has 'breed abundantly', which captures the sense but loses the echo of the first creation. It also moves the main verb to the front ('Bring forth'), where Hebrew puts it last, delaying it until the whole catalogue of life has been named. Rashi, reading 'in the earth', adds that the animals were forbidden to breed in the ark.

There is a textual quirk: the written form is hōṣē', the read form hayṣē' (Ketiv/Qere); both mean 'bring out'. Rashi makes a midrash of the two forms; Radak explains it as grammar alone. And 'the creeper that creeps' repeats one root (rāmaś) twice, which the literal layer keeps.

philological_notes.note: Qere; the written (Ketiv) form is הוצא. Both are Hiphil imperatives 'bring out'. Rashi splits them homiletically; Radak and Ibn Ezra treat it as a spelling variation of the verb with initial yod/waw.
'Swarm, teem'. Used in Genesis 1:20 of water creatures. Radak says it expresses the greatest increase and is used here because few animals leave the ark.
'The creeper that creeps': noun and participle of one root, kept as a repetition.

verses.translation_literal: And Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him.
verses.translation_dramatic: So Noah went out. His sons came with him, and his wife, and the wives of his sons.
verses.directors_commentary:
God's order of verse 16 paired husband and wife; the narrator reports it with the sexes apart again, Noah and his sons first, the women after. Radak guesses that the women, still afraid of the flood, waited for the men to go first. That is his own psychological reading; the Hebrew only gives the order. Use it as a staging cue: the family emerges in a line, the first to step onto the earth after more than a year.

The verse is nearly identical to 7:7 with the one verb reversed, 'entered' to 'went out'. Hebrew has no word for 'came out safe'; the plain verb yāṣāʾ does everything. KJV's 'went forth' is archaic, but keeps the sense.

philological_notes.note: 'And he went out': the answer to ṣēʾ in v16. Noah obeys with the same verb he was given.

verses.translation_literal: Every living thing, every creeper and every bird, all that creeps on the earth, by their families went out from the ark.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every living thing, every creeper, every bird, all that creeps upon the earth — family by family they came out of the ark.
verses.directors_commentary:
The animals leave the way they came, group by group. The key word is lĕmišpəḥōtêhem, 'by their families'. KJV has 'after their kinds', which borrows the min of Genesis 1 ('after its kind'); the Hebrew here is not min but mišpāḥâ, 'family, clan', the word used for human households. ASV and YLT correctly have 'families'. Radak equates it with 'kinds' and Rashi says the animals took on themselves to keep to their own kind, but the word itself is the household word.

The verse piles up nouns in a way English finds untidy: hayyâ, remeś, ʿôp, then a catch-all 'everything that creeps on the earth'. Radak reads the last as including the livestock and wild animals. Say it as a roll-call: the sound of the whole zoo filing out, one family after another.

philological_notes.note: 'By their families'. Not min 'kind' as in Genesis 1. Radak reads it as 'by their kinds, each kind by itself'; Ibn Ezra adds that some said they bred in the ark and each family left unmixed.

verses.translation_literal: And Noah built an altar to YHWH, and took from every clean livestock and from every clean bird, and made burnt offerings go up on the altar.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Noah built an altar to the LORD. He chose from among the clean animals, from among the clean birds, and he lifted them up in fire on the altar.
verses.directors_commentary:
Before he builds a house or plants a field, Noah builds an altar. This is the first altar in the Bible; mizbēaḥ means 'the place of slaughter' (from zābaḥ, to slaughter). He gives the first of what he has to the one who kept him alive, and he does so unprompted: no command is recorded. And here the divine name changes: Elohim commanded in verse 15, but it is YHWH to whom the altar is built.

The offerings are 'ōlôt, 'ascending offerings', wholly consumed on the altar, and KJV's 'burnt offerings' is correct. The word 'clean' has been waiting since 7:2–3, where Noah took seven pairs of clean animals; Rashi comments that Noah was not commanded to bring seven of each in order to sacrifice, but understood it; Ibn Ezra counts the numbers. A modern reader needs to see what that cost: a sacrifice of clean animals when each species was a single pair is a sacrifice of the future breeding stock. Radak reads the act as thanks for rescue. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds that it was the altar where Adam, Cain and Abel had sacrificed, an embellishment, not in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: 'Altar', literally 'place of slaughter'; first altar in the Bible. Radak discusses where Noah built it, and whether it was at the site of Adam's altar.
'Ascending offerings': burnt offerings consumed entirely. Radak records the rabbinic dispute whether Noah's offerings were only these or also peace offerings.
'The clean', the category from 7:2–3 of animals fit for sacrifice and food. Radak says unclean animals are not fit for sacrifice since they are not even fit for eating.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH smelled the soothing aroma, and YHWH said to his heart: I will not again curse the ground any more for the sake of the human, for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth; and I will not again strike down any more every living thing, just as I have done.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD breathed in the soothing aroma. And the LORD said within his heart: Never again will I curse the ground because of humankind — even though the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth. Never again will I strike down every living thing, as I have done.
verses.directors_commentary:
The center of the chapter, and the quietest voice in it. God does not speak to Noah here; he speaks 'to his heart', a private resolution that Noah overhears only because the narrator does. Ramban and Sforno take this to mean the promise was not yet told to Noah; Ibn Ezra, by contrast, takes ʾel as 'with' and says it was revealed later. Either way, play it as a decision made in the stillness after the smoke.

The verse hides a wordplay. 'Soothing' is nîḥōaḥ, from the root nûaḥ, to rest; the name Noah (nōaḥ) is the same root. Noah means 'rest'; his offering is 'a restful aroma'; and the smell brings God to rest from the anger of chapter 6. KJV's 'sweet savour' keeps the pleasure but loses the rest, and with it the echo of the hero's name (see 5:29). Likewise 'smelled' is not a metaphor to be explained away: Ibn Ezra and Radak insist the Torah speaks in human language and means only that the offering was accepted. The same scene appears in the Mesopotamian flood story, where the gods smell the sacrifice and gather round it, so the first audience would have heard it as the familiar beat of the story; the contrast with the older version is that here one God, unforced, chooses mercy.

Then the surprise. In 6:5 the evidence of the heart's 'inclination' was the reason for the flood; here the same fact, 'evil from youth', is the reason not to repeat it. KJV's 'imagination' is archaic for yēṣer, a shaping or inclination, what has been formed (from yāṣar, to shape, as a potter); Ibn Ezra reads it as 'what was formed in him'. The little word kî can be 'for' or 'even though'; Ramban finds in 'from youth' a plea in mitigation. 'Curse' here is qillēl, 'to treat lightly, make contemptible', not the 'arar of 3:17 and 5:29, which KJV also renders 'curse'. And 'any more', 'again', 'again': the repetition is itself the weight, which Rashi takes as an oath.

philological_notes.note: 'The soothing, restful', from the root of Noah's name (nōaḥ). The aroma 'rests' God. Ibn Ezra derives it from mənûḥâ 'rest' and says it means that the anger was quieted.

'Inclination, what is formed': from yāṣar, 'to shape'. Ibn Ezra: the nature formed in him. Radak: it is called yēṣer because it was fashioned with him. KJV's 'imagination' is a misleading archaism here.
'To curse, to treat as light'; a different root from ʾārar, the curse of 3:17. Ibn Ezra links it to the earlier 'cursed is the ground'.

verses.translation_literal: Still, all the days of the earth: seed and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.
verses.translation_dramatic: As long as the earth has days — seed and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night — they will not cease.
verses.directors_commentary:
The flood story ends with a promise in poetry: eight terms in four pairs, a kind of liturgy of the world's rhythm, closing with a verb that plays on 'Sabbath'. Yishbōtû, 'they will cease', is from šābat, the root of Shabbat. The point of the pairs is that the order of the year is a gift that was suspended. Rashi hears an implication in 'day and night shall not cease': during the flood they had, so the ordinary round of light and dark was lost; Radak considers that the clouded sky simply hid it.

The pairs can be read as farming terms (seed and harvest, the two halves of the agricultural year) and weather terms (cold/heat, winter/summer), closed by the widest rhythm of all, day and night. Rashi, in the Talmud's calendar, assigns each to two months of the year, with harvest in spring and heat in late summer. For the first hearers, a farming people dependent on rain and seasons, nothing could be more reassuring. KJV's 'while the earth remaineth' is a fair paraphrase of 'all the days of the earth', but the Hebrew phrase makes the earth itself a thing with days, a lifespan. Ibn Ezra reads from this that the earth has an appointed end. 'Cold' (qōr) and 'winter' (ḥōrep) are two words in the Hebrew where KJV also gives two; Rashi distinguishes them, 'cold' being harsher.

philological_notes.note: 'They will cease, rest': the root of Shabbat. Rashi: from 'shall not cease' we learn that they did cease during the flood, when the heavenly bodies did not mark day from night.
'Cold and heat': Ibn Ezra and Radak read the four pairs as the division of the year first in two (seed, harvest), then in four seasons; Rashi assigns each to a stretch of two months.

events.title: God remembers Noah and sends a wind over the earth
events.narrative_summary: God remembers Noah and all the animals with him in the ark and makes a wind pass over the earth, and the waters subside. The springs of the deep and the floodgates of heaven are shut and the rain is restrained.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 8:3 says the waters decreased 'from the end of a hundred and fifty days'; ch. 7 gives the prevailing as 150 days from 2/17, so this scene starts at the end of evt.gen_7.waters_prevail (about 7/17). The closing of the springs is placed in the same turn (Ramban: at the end of the 150 days). Margin 2 days for the month-counting.

events.title: The waters recede until the mountaintops appear
events.narrative_summary: The waters go back and forth from the earth and keep decreasing from the end of the 150 days until the tenth month.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Runs from the end of the 150 days (7/17) to 10/1 (8:5). With 30-day months 7/17 to 10/1 is 74 days (13 + 30 + 30 + 1; Ramban counts 73 as 'after 73 days'). Margin 2 days for 29/30-day month alternation. Rashi/Radak read the months from the start of the rains (Kislev start), Ramban from 2/17; I follow the text's own calendar of ch. 7 (Ramban, Ibn Ezra's 'tenth month from the Flood').

events.title: The ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat
events.narrative_summary: In the seventh month, on the seventeenth day, the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 2/17 + 150 days = 7/17 in 30-day months (five months), so it begins at the end of evt.gen_7.waters_prevail. Ramban explains the identity of 150 days with the dating of 8:4; Rashi/Radak count the seventh month differently (from Marheshvan = Sivan 17), which I did not follow because it would contradict the 150 days.
events.ancient_year_marker: In the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month

events.title: The tops of the mountains become visible
events.narrative_summary: In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains are seen.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 10/1, i.e. 74 days after 7/17 (see evt.gen_8.waters_recede): offset 74 days from the ark's resting. Ramban counts 73 days. Margin 2 days.
events.ancient_season_marker: In the tenth month, on the first day of the month

events.title: Noah opens the window of the ark
events.narrative_summary: At the end of forty days Noah opens the window he had made in the ark.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'At the end of forty days': Rashi counts from the appearance of the mountaintops (10/1), Radak from the ark resting (which would be 40 days from 7/17, before the tops were seen, and he notes it). I follow Rashi: offset 40 days from mountain_tops_seen (about 11/11). Margin 3 days for the other readings.
events.ancient_season_marker: At the end of forty days

events.title: Noah sends out a raven that goes to and fro
events.narrative_summary: Noah sends out the raven, which flies out and back until the waters dry up from the earth.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Sent as the window is opened (END of that event, no delay in the text). It continues 'until the waters dried' (8:13, year 601 1/1), about 50 days from about 11/11 to 1/1; the duration is an estimate of that span. Ibn Ezra puts the raven's sending on the 10th of Shevat. Margin 2 days.

events.title: Noah sends out a dove, which returns finding no rest
events.narrative_summary: Noah sends out a dove to see whether the waters have abated, but it finds no resting place and returns to the ark, where Noah takes it in.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No delay is stated, but 8:10 says he waited 'yet other seven days', which implies a first seven-day wait after the raven (as Ibn Ezra reads it: seven days after the raven the dove). Offset 7 days from the raven's sending, margin 3 days; the flight lasts hours.

events.title: The dove returns at evening with an olive leaf
events.narrative_summary: After waiting another seven days Noah sends out the dove again; it returns at evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf, and Noah knows the waters have abated.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'He waited yet other seven days' (8:10): offset 7 days from the first flight's start. The dove returns 'at evening time' (8:11; Radak: the same day), so the event spans the day. Margin 1 day.

events.title: Noah sends out the dove a third time and it does not return
events.narrative_summary: After another seven days Noah sends out the dove, and it does not come back to him again.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'He waited yet other seven days' (8:12): offset 7 days from the second flight (about 12/2 by this chain). Margin 1 day. A gap of about a month remains before 8:13 (1/1); the text tells nothing of those days.

events.title: Noah removes the ark's covering and sees dry ground
events.narrative_summary: In Noah's six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters are dried up from the earth; Noah removes the ark's covering and sees that the ground is dry.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A date in the text's own calendar: year 601, month 1, day 1. Counting from the start of the rains (2/17 of year 600; chain of ch. 7 and anchor.flood): 13 remaining days of month 2, then months 3–12, then 1 day to 1/1 = 314 days in 30-day months. I anchor on the START of waters_prevail with offset 314 days, margin 3 days. Radak notes the new year begins at Tishri (so 601 begins at the first month); the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan says 'Tishri'.
events.ancient_year_marker: In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first day of the month

events.title: The earth is fully dry
events.narrative_summary: In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day, the earth is dry.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 2/27 of year 601: 56 days after 1/1 (29 days to the end of month 1 plus 27 = 56 in 30-day months... counting 1/1 to 2/1 as 30 days, then 26 more). Total from 2/17 of year 600: 370 days, a year and about 10 days (Radak citing Genesis Rabbah on the ten days by which the solar year exceeds the lunar). Margin 3 days.
events.ancient_season_marker: In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month

events.title: God tells Noah to leave the ark with everyone and everything
events.narrative_summary: God tells Noah to go out of the ark with his wife, his sons and their wives, and to bring out every living thing so that they may swarm, be fruitful and multiply on the earth.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 8:15 follows 8:14 with no marker of delay, so it starts at the end of the day on which the earth is dry. Radak says Noah was not told to leave at 8:13 because the ground was still muddy. A speech: a few minutes; margin 1 day.

events.title: Noah and all the animals go out of the ark
events.narrative_summary: Noah goes out with his wife, his sons and their wives, and every animal, creeping thing and bird goes out of the ark by families.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Direct obedience to the command of 8:16–17 with no delay in the text; starts at the END of the command. Duration is an estimate of a few hours for the whole company; margin 1 day.

events.title: Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings
events.narrative_summary: Noah builds an altar to the LORD and offers burnt offerings on it from every clean animal and clean bird.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the leaving of the ark with no stated delay (8:20). Building an altar and sacrificing take hours; margin 2 days for the time between disembarking and the offering, which the text leaves open.

events.title: The LORD smells the pleasing aroma and resolves not to curse the ground again
events.narrative_summary: The LORD smells the soothing aroma and says in his heart that he will not again curse the ground because of humankind, nor strike down every living thing, and that seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will not cease.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The smelling follows the offering immediately (8:21), so it starts at the END of the offering; a few minutes for the inner speech. Margin 1 hour.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: God commands Noah to go out of the ark with his family and the animals (8:16–17), and Noah goes out with them as commanded (8:18–19).
Because God remembers Noah and sends a wind, the waters turn back and decrease (8:1–3).
The LORD smells the soothing aroma of Noah's burnt offerings and so resolves never again to curse the ground (8:20–21).

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew mizbēaḥ, from zābaḥ, 'to slaughter for sacrifice': a place of sacrifice.
entities.summary_bio: The altar Noah built to the LORD after leaving the ark. On it he offered burnt offerings of every clean animal and bird, and the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ʿălēh zayit, a leaf of the olive tree, here freshly plucked (tāraf).
entities.summary_bio: The freshly plucked olive leaf the dove carried back at evening. It told Noah that the waters had abated from the earth.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew yônâ, the dove; the name is of uncertain origin and may imitate its cooing.
entities.summary_bio: The bird Noah sent out three times to learn whether the waters had abated. It returned empty, then with an olive leaf, and the third time did not return.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ʿōrēb, the raven, a dark bird; the name is probably connected with the root for blackness or evening.
entities.summary_bio: The first bird Noah sent out of the ark. It flew to and fro until the waters dried up, and the text does not say it returned.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably from Akkadian Urartu, the highland kingdom north of Assyria; the name refers to a region rather than one peak.
entities.summary_bio: The mountain range where the ark came to rest in the seventh month of the flood. The text names a range, not a single summit.

components.evidence_explanation: Gen 8:20: Noah built an altar to the LORD.

components.label_value: Resting on the mountains of Ararat
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 8:4: the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat on the seventeenth day of the seventh month.

components.label_value: Gone from the ark for good
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 8:12: Noah sent out the dove and it did not return to him again.
Gen 8:14: in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day, the earth was dry.

components.label_value: Out of the ark, on the mountains of Ararat
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 8:18: Noah went out of the ark; the ark had rested on Ararat (8:4).
Gen 8:21: the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma and spoke in his heart.

components.label_value: Never again to curse the ground or strike all living things
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 8:21: 'I will never again curse the ground... nor strike down every living thing.'

systems.name: Burnt offering
systems.ancient_near_east_context: The ʿōlâ, 'that which goes up', was wholly consumed on the altar, so that all of it rose to the deity. It was the commonest sacrifice in Israel and in neighbouring cults, and the Mesopotamian flood hero likewise offers after the flood.
rules_and_mechanics: Only clean animals and birds may be offered.
The offering is burned entire on an altar.
The smoke is a 'pleasing aroma' (rêaḥ hannîḥōaḥ) to the deity.
The offerer builds the altar to the deity addressed.

systems.name: God remembers
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In biblical idiom God 'remembering' means turning to act on behalf of those in his covenant care (Gen 19:29; 30:22; Exod 2:24). Mesopotamian flood stories likewise end with the gods' attention returning to the survivors.
rules_and_mechanics: Remembering is an action, not mental recall.
It marks the turn from judgment to rescue.
It is followed by concrete intervention, here the wind and the closing of the deep.

systems.name: Scouting for land with birds
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the Mesopotamian flood accounts (Gilgamesh XI, Atrahasis tradition) the hero also releases birds, a dove, a swallow and a raven, to find dry land. Sailors of the ancient world used birds the same way.
rules_and_mechanics: A bird is sent out of the vessel and its return or absence is read as a sign.
A bird that comes back means no land is yet fit to settle.
A bird that does not return means land is available.
Waiting periods of seven days separate the releases.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Noah builds an altar to the LORD.
system_instances.significance_note: His first act on the renewed earth is worship.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Noah offers burnt offerings of clean animals and birds, and the LORD smells the pleasing aroma.
system_instances.significance_note: The offering prompts the LORD's resolve never again to curse the ground.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Noah takes from every clean animal and clean bird for the offering.
system_instances.significance_note: The seven pairs of clean animals taken aboard (7:2) allow a sacrifice without ending any species.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The dove finds no resting place and Noah takes her back into the ark.
system_instances.significance_note: Shows the water still covers the whole ground.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The dove returns at evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf.
system_instances.significance_note: Tells Noah the waters have abated and plants are growing again; the olive leaf later became a symbol of peace.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The dove does not come back.
system_instances.significance_note: Shows dry land can now support life and prepares the exit from the ark.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God tells Noah to go out with his family and to bring out every creature so that they may swarm, be fruitful and multiply.
system_instances.significance_note: Noah leaves only on God's word, as he entered on it; the creation blessing is renewed.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God sends a wind over the earth, the deep and the heavens are closed, and the waters subside.
system_instances.significance_note: Turns the story from judgment to deliverance and marks the start of the earth's recovery.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD resolves never again to curse the ground or strike down all living things, and the seasons and day and night will not cease.
system_instances.significance_note: Sets the terms of the post-flood world, despite human evil, and leads into the covenant of chapter 9.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The raven goes to and fro until the waters dry up; no report is given.
system_instances.significance_note: The first test of the land gives Noah no usable answer.

edges.description: God tells Noah to go out of the ark with his wife, sons and sons' wives.
God remembers Noah and all in the ark and acts to end the flood.
Noah builds an altar to the LORD and offers burnt offerings on it.
Noah sends the dove out to see whether the waters have abated.
Noah sends the raven out of the ark.
Noah reaches out and brings the exhausted dove back into the ark.
The LORD resolves not to curse the ground again on account of humankind, nor to strike down all living things.
